Can an image made of shapes beat WebP?

Reduce a photograph to regions, code the boundaries, ship the geometry. Five rounds of measurement against the codecs that already exist. The answer is no — with one narrow exception, and it is not worth adopting a format for.

Never beaten, at any rate on this image.

Physics, collective systems, vision, spacecraft.

The rate–distortion curve

Every point is one encoder setting on one 512×288 photograph, measured on a single RGB PSNR definition. Down and to the right is better. Both codecs are at their strong settings (cwebp -m 6, avifenc -s 0), not CLI defaults — running WebP on its default was worth more than the entire effect this study once claimed. The shape coder now lies on the WebP curve below ~26 dB, alternating sign between samples, and falls behind above it. AVIF sits under both across the whole range.

shape coder WebP AVIF curves meet ≈26.1 dB

The same picture, at the same fidelity

Three fidelity bands. Within each band every encoder produces the same measured quality, so the only thing that differs is the byte count — and what the degradation looks like, which PSNR cannot see. The bar under each figure is its weight.

Band A

~28.7 dB

The evaluation fidelity. The shape coder is behind a properly configured WebP and 1.41× behind AVIF. What the project ships is 9.7× heavier than the WebP of the same picture.

Band B

~26.4 dB

The low-rate band, where the two representations come closest: fewer, larger regions keep the perimeter tax small while a block codec keeps paying per-block overhead. This is the shape coder's best sample point on the whole curve, and adjacent samples put it back behind.

Band C

~24 dB

The floor. The merge bottoms out near 150 regions; WebP bottoms out at q0. Note the failure modes diverge completely — posterized flat regions against blur and blocking. PSNR scores them equal; an eye would not.

The shape coder is second, and it does not exist. It is a measured cross-entropy bound from a research segmenter — no container, no header, no bitstream. What the repository actually ships is last, behind a 1996 PNG by 4× and a 1992 JPEG by 6×.

What was tried and killed

Eight of sixteen. Each was required to produce a mechanism, a runnable experiment and a predicted number before it was run — so every rejection carries a measurement rather than an opinion.

MechanismResult
Let the decoder regrow regions — “don’t serialize”collective systemsProvably a rename. Any region reconstructible from decoded pixels is a function of the causal past, so it is a context model — bounded by H(X | causal past). ≥ 16.2 KB.
PDE diffusion inpainting (Weickert R-EED)physics / biologyThe literal morphogenesis codec. Seed mask alone costs 9.5 KB — over the wall before a single colour is sent. Total ~21–25 KB.
Centroidal Voronoi / Lloyd relaxationphysics44.3 KB.
Seeds derived by the decoder — geometry costs exactly zerophysicsColours alone still 17.6 KB. Collapses to downsample-then-upsample.
Shared dictionary across a best-case corpuscompressionBuilt to favour shapes: 8 images, one shared palette, identical dimensions. Shapes gain 1.02×, WebP 1.01×. The asymmetry does not exist.
Hyperspectral amortization — 200 bands, geometry freespace systemsGeometry falls to 2% of the budget and shapes still lose 3.4–14.5×.
Portilla-Simoncelli texture synthesisvision~5–6 KB — the only sub-wall number found anywhere. But PSNR collapses to ~18 dB. It is a generative texture codec, not a shape format.
Phase transition in palette sizephysicsSwept n = 2…256. bpp monotonic. No knee, no regime where shapes get cheap.

Nine claims this research killed — its own

Every one was produced by this investigation, believed, written into a README, then falsified by a later measurement in the same investigation. Six of the nine were the same error: the wrong baseline, always in the direction that flattered the hypothesis. The last three were found only after the study looked finished.

  1. “Beats WebP by 31%”Lossy pipeline compared against WebP in lossless mode. At matched fidelity it is 1.41× behind.
  2. “We’re at the entropy floor”Order-3 was sample-starved, not diluted — 36 samples per context. Mixing recovers it: 16.2 KB.
  3. “Geometry alone costs 19.2 KB”Artifact of my own weak segmenter. A proper energy-minimizing one costs 9.0 KB.
  4. “Renders at 8K for the same bytes”Fake vectorness. A rect cover of a quantized grid is nearest-neighbour upscaling.
  5. “9.8× smaller than the source”The win was the downscale. Against the same pixels it is 6.9× larger.
  6. “3–9% better at low rate”Taken from one run of a nondeterministic merge, interpolated by eye. Truth: 1–6%.
  7. “The merge is deterministic now”Fixed one instance, not the class. Two more map-iteration randomizers survived, found only at 4K.
  8. “1–6% better at low rate”The baseline was cwebp on its default -m 4. At -m 6 it is a wash that alternates sign.
  9. “Beats WebP below 29.2 dB”True at 512×288 only. The deficit grows monotonically with resolution — +19.3% at 4K.
None was caught by reasoning. Each was caught by a later measurement that happened to overlap. The only structural defence that worked was requiring every investigating agent to reproduce the shared evaluation before its findings were believed — which caught a false headline in flight, from an agent that had silently substituted a different image.

So where does this leave shapes?

Not as a codec. The byte win is 1–6% over the second-best format, in a band where the best format leads by 8–52%, and it sits inside the margin a real container would erase. But the win lands in the same place as everything shapes offer that rasters cannot — resolution-independent geometry, drawing with no decode step, per-region addressability, recolouring by palette entry — which is thumbnails, placeholders, e-ink, low-power displays and starved links. The representation is the product. The compression never was.
